pages.mainText: Amazon Relay Requirements Commercial trucking insurance and onboarding requirements for carriers considering Amazon Relay. Amazon Relay: carrier and insurance requirements Amazon sets its own onboarding standards. Meeting an insurance minimum does not guarantee acceptance into Relay. Check Amazon's current requirements before purchasing coverage or committing to equipment. Carrier eligibility Amazon's published requirements include a DOT number with interstate authority active for at least 180 days, a valid MC number, and authorization as a for-hire property carrier. Amazon also checks safety ratings, BASIC scores and driver and vehicle violation rates. Applications may begin before the tenure requirement is met. Published U.S. insurance minimums Commercial general liability: $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate. Commercial auto liability: $1 million per occurrence, including $50,000 trailer replacement coverage. Motor truck cargo: at least $100,000. Workers' compensation in the jurisdictions where the company operates. Employer liability: at least $100,000 per occurrence. Match coverage to the vehicle and program Commercial auto liability addresses covered injury or property damage involving the insured truck. Motor truck cargo addresses covered loss or damage to freight. General liability addresses certain non-auto business exposures; Amazon lists it as a separate Relay requirement, not a replacement for auto or cargo coverage. Amazon's insurance guide specifically associates $50,000 trailer interchange coverage with semi-truck operations, while its general onboarding list uses the broader term trailer replacement coverage. Confirm the applicable coverage form for your equipment and program with Amazon and your insurer. Do not assume a box-truck operation and a tractor pulling someone else's trailer need identical endorsements. Relay standards and government minimums Amazon's platform standards are separate from government insurance requirements. FMCSA's filing chart varies by authority, cargo and vehicle type. For example, it lists $750,000 in bodily injury/property damage coverage for non-hazardous, for-hire property carriers using vehicles with a GVWR of at least 10,001 pounds, versus Relay's $1 million auto liability minimum. Satisfying a federal filing requirement does not establish Relay eligibility or satisfy every contract. Prepare for an insurance review Bring your operating details and Amazon's current requirements to your agent. Review limits, exclusions, effective dates and required documentation. A quote or certificate does not itself change policy coverage. Amazon verifies insurance during onboarding, and its compliance vendor obtains the certificate from the agent, broker or insurer on file. Keep renewal details current. Motive can help review your commercial truck insurance ; Amazon makes the platform approval decision. Requirements checked November 10, 2026. Sources: Amazon Relay's official requirements and FAQ , Amazon's onboarding requirements , Amazon's insurance guide , and FMCSA's filing requirements . Amazon controls eligibility and can change its standards.

Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance When clients hire an executive transportation company, they expect professionalism from pickup to destination. Your insurance should be approached with the same level of attention. This guide explains coverage considerations for black car, limousine, chauffeur, and executive transportation businesses, including vehicle values, passengers, drivers, and contracts. Who needs black car insurance? Black car insurance may apply to businesses providing: Executive transportation Corporate transportation Limousine services Chauffeur services Private car services Airport transportation VIP transportation Event transportation Hourly transportation Prearranged passenger service The specific insurance needs depend on how the company operates. A single owner-driven luxury sedan is not the same risk as a fleet of SUVs and limousines serving corporate accounts. Commercial auto for black car operations Personal auto insurance is generally not designed for vehicles being used as part of a commercial passenger transportation business. Commercial auto coverage should reflect the vehicle's business use. Underwriters may examine: Vehicle type Vehicle value Passenger capacity Driver history Operating area Annual mileage Airport activity Years in business Contracts Claims history The details matter. A luxury SUV used for executive transportation presents a different insurance profile from an ordinary passenger vehicle used for personal commuting. Passenger exposure Executive transportation companies are responsible for people. That passenger exposure should be part of the insurance conversation from the beginning. Passenger volume, vehicle capacity, interstate trips and the structure of the operation can affect applicable insurance requirements and underwriting. Limousine insurance Limousines can create additional insurance considerations because of: Vehicle configuration Passenger capacity Vehicle value Specialty equipment Operating hours Event transportation Alcohol-related exposures Driver requirements Long-distance trips These factors should be disclosed accurately when requesting limousine insurance. An insurance comparison is not meaningful if the business use, vehicles, or passenger responsibilities have been described incorrectly. Airport and corporate transportation Many black car companies build their business around airports and corporate clients. That can mean: Frequent airport trips Advance reservations Corporate agreements Hotel partnerships Travel-management relationships High annual mileage Multiple drivers Late-night or early-morning operations Insurance should evolve with those contracts. A company that began with one vehicle and private clients may need a different structure once it begins servicing larger commercial accounts. Physical damage for high-value vehicles Executive transportation fleets frequently use late-model SUVs, sedans and specialty vehicles. Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles from covered collision and comprehensive losses. Vehicle valuation and deductible choices deserve particular attention when the fleet includes high-value vehicles. General liability and business exposure Your risk does not always begin and end inside the vehicle. General liability may be relevant for certain third-party claims connected to business operations outside normal automobile liability. Workers' compensation A company employing chauffeurs, dispatchers or other staff should also review workers' compensation requirements and employee exposures. Umbrella and excess liability Executive transportation companies may work with clients or contracts requiring higher liability limits. Umbrella or excess liability can provide additional limits above certain underlying policies when appropriate and available. What affects black car insurance cost? Insurance carriers may review: Number of vehicles Luxury vehicle values Vehicle age Passenger capacity Driver age and experience Motor vehicle records Claims history Operating radius Airport use Annual mileage Hours of operation Corporate contracts Interstate travel Requested limits Deductibles From one black car to a transportation fleet Growth changes the insurance problem. Review the operation as a transportation business rather than treating each vehicle as an unrelated policy decision. Insurance that matches the service Your clients expect a professional driver. A professional vehicle. A professional experience. Your insurance program should receive the same consideration. The most useful review follows the service from reservation and pickup through the completed trip. pages.mainText: BMC-84 vs BMC-85 Compare BMC-84 bonds and BMC-85 trusts for transportation financial responsibility. BMC-84 bond or BMC-85 trust? FMCSA lists a $75,000 surety bond or trust fund requirement for property and household-goods brokers. BMC-84 and BMC-85 are alternative financial-responsibility filings, not personal auto insurance policies. BMC-84: surety bond A surety provider files the BMC-84 bond. Compare the premium, underwriting requirements, collateral and indemnity terms. The $75,000 bond amount is not a quoted annual premium; payment and reimbursement obligations depend on the agreement. BMC-85: trust fund An eligible financial institution files the BMC-85 trust agreement. Review how the trust is funded, which assets qualify, fees and the conditions for releasing funds. Do not assume a low advertised fee replaces the required financial security. Account for the 2026 rules FMCSA's updated broker and freight-forwarder financial-responsibility requirements took effect January 16, 2026. They address eligible trust providers, available assets and procedures when financial security falls below $75,000. Confirm your provider's eligibility and current filing status. Compare the full obligation Ask your provider about upfront funding, ongoing costs, claims handling and cancellation. Discuss your operation with Motive before selecting an arrangement. mainEntity.name: Where can a new box truck carrier look for loads?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common starting points include load boards, freight brokers that accept your authority profile, direct outreach to local shippers, and referrals from existing business relationships. Confirm that each opportunity fits your operating authority, equipment, service area, and insurance before accepting it.

mainEntity.name: How should I compare two loads?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compare total pay against every mile and expense attached to the trip—not only loaded miles. Include deadhead to pickup, repositioning after delivery, tolls, operating cost, schedule requirements, and payment terms. The calculator above can organize those inputs consistently.

mainEntity.name: What should I ask before accepting a box truck load?

acceptedAnswer.text: Confirm the commodity, piece count, dimensions, weight, declared value where relevant, loading method, securement, pickup and delivery appointments, stops, driver-assist requirements, total pay, accessorial process, required documents, and payment terms.

mainEntity.name: How can I verify a freight broker?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use independent FMCSA records to compare the company’s legal identity, USDOT or MC information, authority, and available licensing and insurance data. Verify unexpected contact or payment changes through a previously confirmed channel before dispatch.

mainEntity.name: Do Illinois intrastate carriers need separate authority?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Illinois Commerce Commission states that businesses engaging in for-hire transportation of property wholly within Illinois generally need a Public Carrier Certificate unless an exemption applies. Federal authority does not automatically replace an Illinois requirement for intrastate operations.

mainEntity.name: When does direct freight make sense?

acceptedAnswer.text: Direct freight can make sense when you can define a reliable service area, equipment fit, schedule, and rate, then consistently manage customer communication, delivery, documentation, and invoicing. It normally requires more prospecting and follow-up than broker freight.

The work may reach a carrier through a broker, a load board, a direct shipper relationship, or a recurring route agreement. Before dispatch, the carrier should confirm the commodity, dimensions, weight, handling requirements, pickup and delivery appointments, total route miles, payment terms, and required documentation. The shipment is not financially complete when the truck unloads—it closes when the signed delivery record is accepted and the invoice is paid. 01 Shipment created The customer defines the freight, locations, schedule, and service expectations. 02 Carrier selected The broker or shipper confirms equipment fit, authority, insurance, availability, and price. 03 Terms documented The carrier receives written load details and resolves discrepancies before moving. 04 Freight delivered The driver protects the cargo, communicates exceptions, and obtains proof of delivery. 05 Payment closed The carrier submits the required documents and tracks the invoice through payment. The broker sells and manages the shipper relationship; the carrier supplies the truck, driver, and transportation service. Good broker relationships are built on accurate equipment information, fast communication, reliable appointment performance, clean paperwork, and honest updates when a problem occurs. Before accepting a load, confirm exactly who is paying you, what the truck must do, and which documents trigger payment. See the broker setup packet → Broker relationship One load can become a repeat lane. After successful delivery, send the required documents promptly, confirm receipt, and tell the broker which lanes, days, and equipment configurations you can cover again. 04 / Preparation Broker Setup Packet Prepare one controlled folder before contacting brokers. Use the same legal business name and address shown in your carrier registration, tax, banking, and insurance records. Mismatched names or outdated documents can delay setup and payment. As you describe the loads and routes you plan to run, use our box truck insurance quote preparation guide to organize the information for your request. Insurance evidence A current certificate of insurance and the agent contact who can handle certificate requests or coverage questions. Equipment profile Interior dimensions, door opening, payload limit, dock height, liftgate, pallet jack, straps, blankets, and service radius. Operating documents Any authority, registration, or other document the broker reasonably requests for the shipment and operating model. Process contacts Who accepts loads, who handles tracking, who sends proof of delivery, and who follows invoices through payment. Carrier details Equipment profile Coverage documents Contacts 05 / Available freight Load Boards Load boards organize posted freight by origin, destination, date, equipment, and other filters. They can help fill open capacity, but a listing is only a lead—not proof that the load fits your truck or produces a profit. Build narrow searches around the cities you can reach on time, your true cargo dimensions and payload, and where the truck will be positioned after delivery. Save repeat searches, record which contacts provide usable box-truck freight, and compare the complete trip before calling. Filter for straight truck or box truck equipment and verify the actual dimensions with the contact. Check pickup distance, appointment windows, delivery requirements, and likely repositioning miles. Ask whether the load requires a dock, liftgate, pallet jack, driver assist, inside delivery, or multiple stops. Confirm the broker or shipper identity independently before sending documents or accepting instructions. Get the agreed rate and service requirements in writing before dispatch. How to evaluate a load → 06 / The decision How to Evaluate a Load Loaded-mile rate alone can hide an expensive trip. Add the miles from your current position to pickup, the loaded route, and the likely distance to parking or the next freight market. Then account for fuel, maintenance reserve, tires, tolls, payroll or driver compensation, insurance allocation, financing, dispatch or factoring fees, and other trip-specific expenses. Operational fit matters too. A rate that looks acceptable can fail if detention consumes the next appointment, the freight does not fit through the door, the receiver requires equipment you do not carry, or the delivery leaves the truck far from the next opportunity. Equipment fit Confirm cargo dimensions, total weight, piece count, loading method, securement, and special handling. Schedule fit Check pickup and delivery windows, drive time, traffic, breaks, parking, and the effect on the next commitment. Economic fit Compare pay with total miles and all variable or allocated operating costs—not only fuel. Price every early load with the same cost discipline you expect to use later. Protect service performance: communicate early, preserve documents, and avoid accepting freight you cannot execute. Build direct-customer outreach alongside broker and load-board activity so one channel does not control the business. Review startup fundamentals → 09 / Due diligence Broker Vetting Verify the company through an independent source rather than relying only on a posting, email signature, caller ID, or document sent by the person offering the load. FMCSA’s free SAFER Company Snapshot provides company identification and safety information, while Licensing & Insurance information can help confirm authority and filings. Compare the legal name, USDOT or MC number, phone number, email domain, and payment instructions. If contact or banking information changes unexpectedly, stop and verify through a previously confirmed channel. Read the broker agreement and rate confirmation before dispatch, including accessorial approval, claims, document submission, and payment provisions. FMCSA SAFER Company Snapshot FMCSA licensing and insurance guidance Decision checkpoint Verify before dispatch. Resolve identity, authority, rate, service, and payment discrepancies before the truck moves. Urgency is not a substitute for verification. 10 / Pricing Rate Negotiation Negotiation starts before the call. Know your total route miles, estimated operating cost, minimum acceptable contribution, schedule limits, and equipment advantages. A defensible counteroffer connects the requested rate to a specific cost or service requirement. State the equipment fit Explain the box size, payload, liftgate, pallet jack, securement, or delivery capability that matches the shipment. Name the complete route Include pickup deadhead, loaded miles, delivery repositioning, toll exposure, and additional stops. Price added service Clarify detention, driver assist, inside delivery, liftgate use, extra stops, redelivery, or schedule changes before accepting them. Confirm the agreement Do not rely on a verbal number. Review the final written rate confirmation and request corrections before dispatch. 11 / Own the relationship Direct Shippers Direct freight begins with a specific service promise: what you move, where you operate, which equipment you provide, when you are available, and how the customer receives delivery updates and documents. Build a prospect list from businesses whose shipment profile fits the truck. Contact the person responsible for shipping, logistics, operations, purchasing, or branch management. Ask about recurring problems—overflow, urgent replenishment, scheduled transfers, final-mile appointments, returns, or routes that do not fit a larger trailer—before offering a solution. Direct work also transfers more responsibility to the carrier. Establish written service terms, credit and payment procedures, cargo information, insurance requirements, points of contact, proof-of-delivery expectations, and a process for exceptions. Explore Illinois customer strategy → 12 / Local market Chicago & Illinois Customer Strategy Organize prospecting by operating zone rather than chasing unrelated businesses across the state. A carrier might define separate zones for Chicago neighborhoods, the suburban industrial corridors, northern Illinois, central Illinois, or specific repeat lanes—but should only promise areas it can serve consistently. Potential box-truck customers can include distributors, manufacturers, commercial suppliers, printers and sign companies, furniture and fixture businesses, event or rental companies, restoration suppliers, and businesses that transfer inventory between branches. The right prospect is determined by freight dimensions, weight, handling, schedule, and service needs—not simply the customer’s industry. Create a list of 25–50 businesses within one practical service zone. Record the shipping contact, freight type, dock or liftgate needs, delivery area, and likely schedule. Lead with one relevant service instead of a general statement that you own a truck. Use a consistent follow-up schedule and record every conversation. Review insurance, authority, and contract requirements before agreeing to the first shipment. 13 / Repeat freight Dedicated Routes A dedicated route is recurring work with a defined frequency, service area, or customer schedule. Consistency can improve planning, but only when the agreement accounts for the entire commitment: reserved truck time, empty repositioning, seasonal volume, wait time, extra stops, handling, backup expectations, and payment terms. Before quoting, run the proposed route as a complete weekly or monthly service. Estimate total miles and hours, identify days when the truck cannot accept other work, and decide how cancellations or added stops are handled. Start with a trial period when possible, measure actual time and cost, and review the rate before committing long term. 14 / Channel comparison Broker Freight vs Direct Freight Both channels can work. Compare them by the role each plays in your freight mix. Dimension Broker freight Direct freight Speed to find freight Often faster once onboarded Usually requires prospecting first Relationship ownership Broker manages the shipper relationship Carrier owns the customer relationship Rate control Negotiate an offered lane or load Build and present your own service price Repeatability Depends on broker freight and performance Can become scheduled recurring work Sales effort Lower after broker setup Higher outreach and follow-up commitment Payment workflow Rate confirmation, POD, broker invoice Customer terms, POD, direct invoice Best use Fill capacity and develop lanes Build durable customer accounts 15 / Close the loop Payment & POD Workflow Set up the payment file when the load is booked—not after delivery. Save the signed rate confirmation or customer order, pickup documentation, delivery instructions, receipts, approved accessorials, and the correct billing contact in one load folder. Before pickup: confirm the legal payer, agreed amount, invoice method, required references, accessorial approval process, and payment terms. At pickup: compare the freight with the paperwork and record exceptions before leaving. At delivery: obtain a legible signed proof of delivery and document shortages, damage, refused freight, or schedule issues. After delivery: submit the invoice and every required attachment through the specified portal or email. Until paid: confirm receipt, record the due date, follow up consistently, and preserve the complete communication trail. Confirm Deliver Document Invoice 16 / Avoid the traps Common Mistakes 01 Taking a load without pricing the full trip Deadhead to pickup, tolls, delivery repositioning, handling time, and the next available lane all belong to the decision. 02 Accepting freight before confirming equipment fit Verify dimensions, weight, door clearance, loading method, securement, liftgate needs, and every stop before dispatch. 03 Depending on one freight source Use broker relationships and load boards for available freight while steadily building direct and recurring customers. 04 Treating urgency as verification Independently confirm the company, authority, contact information, written terms, and payment instructions before moving. 05 Skipping the paperwork trail Preserve the rate confirmation, pickup records, approved accessorials, proof of delivery, invoice, and follow-up history. 06 Promising a service area that is too large Reliable coverage of a focused area is more useful to a customer than inconsistent statewide availability. 17 / Build momentum 30-Day Freight Acquisition Plan Use the first month to build a repeatable operating and sales process—not to accept every available shipment. Week 1 Get Load-Ready Confirm active authority and insurance requirements, document truck dimensions and payload, calculate operating cost, define a service zone, assemble the carrier packet, and create one load folder template. Week 2 Build Broker Relationships Identify brokers that handle your equipment and lanes, ask about onboarding standards, complete eligible setups, create saved load searches, and track every contact in one pipeline. Week 3 Prospect Direct Shippers Build a focused local prospect list, identify shipping or operations contacts, make a specific service offer, record freight requirements, and schedule follow-up rather than relying on one call. Week 4 Build Repeat Freight Review quoted and completed loads, compare estimated costs with actual results, submit documents promptly, ask successful contacts about the next shipment, and narrow the lanes and customer types worth repeating. 18 / Action workspace Freight-Ready Checklist Organize the business, carrier, truck, broker, pricing, and customer details you may need before pursuing freight. 0 / 32 complete 0% Reset Checklist Business Ready 0 / 5 Legal business name finalized Business phone and email ready W-9 available Banking/payment information organized Basic company description prepared Carrier Information 0 / 5 USDOT information available where applicable Authority information available where applicable Authority status checked Insurance certificate available Equipment information documented Truck & Equipment 0 / 5 Truck dimensions documented Payload/capacity understood Liftgate status documented Pallet jack/equipment availability documented Photos of truck available if requested Broker Ready 0 / 6 Carrier packet folder created COI ready W-9 ready Broker agreement review process established Rate confirmation review process established POD submission process established Load Evaluation 0 / 5 Operating cost per mile calculated Minimum acceptable margin defined Maximum acceptable deadhead considered Fuel/toll assumptions understood Load details verification process established Direct Customer Ready 0 / 6 Target customer type selected Service area defined Service offering clearly written Prospect list started Outreach method selected Follow-up system established Freight-Ready Checklist Complete You have organized the major business, carrier, equipment, broker, load-evaluation, and customer-development items covered in this guide. 19 / Questions Box Truck Freight Questions Use these answers as a starting point, then verify each opportunity against your authority, equipment, insurance, operating costs, and written load terms. Where can a new box truck carrier look for loads? Common starting points include load boards, freight brokers that accept your authority profile, direct outreach to local shippers, and referrals from existing business relationships. Confirm that each opportunity fits your operating authority, equipment, service area, and insurance before accepting it. How should I compare two loads? Compare total pay against every mile and expense attached to the trip—not only loaded miles. Include deadhead to pickup, repositioning after delivery, tolls, operating cost, schedule requirements, and payment terms. The calculator above can organize those inputs consistently. What should I ask before accepting a box truck load? Confirm the commodity, piece count, dimensions, weight, declared value where relevant, loading method, securement, pickup and delivery appointments, stops, driver-assist requirements, total pay, accessorial process, required documents, and payment terms. How can I verify a freight broker? Use independent FMCSA records to compare the company’s legal identity, USDOT or MC information, authority, and available licensing and insurance data. Verify unexpected contact or payment changes through a previously confirmed channel before dispatch. Do Illinois intrastate carriers need separate authority? The Illinois Commerce Commission states that businesses engaging in for-hire transportation of property wholly within Illinois generally need a Public Carrier Certificate unless an exemption applies. Federal authority does not automatically replace an Illinois requirement for intrastate operations. When does direct freight make sense? Direct freight can make sense when you can define a reliable service area, equipment fit, schedule, and rate, then consistently manage customer communication, delivery, documentation, and invoicing. It normally requires more prospecting and follow-up than broker freight. 20 / Verify requirements Official Sources Rules and registration systems change. Use the official agencies below to verify authority, insurance filing, Illinois intrastate, and tax-document requirements for your operation. pages.mainText: Box Truck Operating Costs in Matteson Get the Weekly Worksheet The load payment is revenue. Your earnings are what remain after the business pays its bills. When reviewing insurance as an operating expense, use our box truck insurance quote preparation guide to prepare consistent details for comparing coverage. Before you leave a warehouse job, finance a truck, or accept your first delivery, answer one question: How much does this business need to bring in to pay its expenses—and pay you? For a prospective box truck owner-operator in Matteson, a weekly revenue screenshot leaves too much unanswered. It doesn’t show empty return trips, loading delays, repair bills, insurance payments, or invoices that haven’t been collected. This guide explains how to evaluate those costs before committing your savings. 01 / Owner guide What does it cost to operate a box truck? Box truck operating costs include fuel, maintenance, tires, insurance, truck payments or depreciation, parking, tolls, registration, business administration, and any employees or contractors. Your actual costs depend on the truck and the operation. A local delivery business and an interstate freight business should not use the same budget simply because both operate a 26-foot box truck. Separate your expenses into three groups: Cost group What to include Why it matters Recurring costs Insurance, truck payment, parking, software, bookkeeping These bills can continue during a slow week. Operating costs Fuel, tolls, maintenance, tires, delivery-related charges These change with mileage, usage, and the work accepted. Reserves and owner compensation Repair reserve, replacement savings, taxes, and payment for your work Cash left in the account is not automatically available to spend. Avoid counting the same expense twice. For example, a cash-flow budget tracks loan payments, while an accounting profit calculation treats financing and depreciation differently. An accountant can help establish the right method. 02 / Owner guide How deadhead miles reduce box truck revenue per mile Empty miles still use fuel, time, and equipment. Include them in the cost of the complete trip. Deadhead miles are miles driven without a paying load. They can include traveling to a pickup, repositioning after delivery, or returning to your operating base. Here is a worked example—not an actual load listing or a claim about available Matteson freight rates: A customer pays $640 for a delivery covering 200 loaded miles. Trip outcome Total miles Gross revenue per total mile Count only the loaded movement 200 $3.20 Add 100 unpaid miles 300 $2.13 Return empty another 200 miles 400 $1.60 The payment never changed. The amount of driving required to earn it did. Calculate revenue against all miles the job creates. Then subtract expenses. A load that looks attractive on loaded mileage alone can look very different after the return trip. A possible return load should remain a possibility in your budget until it is booked. 03 / Owner guide What fuel can take out of a load payment The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported an average Midwest on-highway diesel price of $6.259 per gallon for the week of October 12, 2026 . This is a dated regional benchmark, not a price quote from a Matteson fuel station. Source: EIA diesel fuel prices Using that benchmark, a 400-mile trip produces the following calculation: Assumed fuel economy Fuel required Estimated fuel expense 8 miles per gallon 50 gallons $312.95 10 miles per gallon 40 gallons $250.36 12 miles per gallon Approximately 33.33 gallons $208.63 These fuel-economy figures are calculation assumptions, not specifications for your truck. In the 10-mpg example, $640 in revenue becomes $389.64 after fuel alone . Insurance, maintenance, tolls, truck ownership costs, and compensation for the operator still need to come out. Use fuel receipts and measured mileage to build your own numbers. If your truck runs on gasoline, use gasoline prices rather than this diesel benchmark. 04 / Owner guide Loading delays affect more than your schedule A delivery can occupy your truck even while the odometer is barely moving. FMCSA summarizes a 2014 study that found detention at approximately one in ten stops , with an average 1.4 hours beyond a two-hour loading and unloading threshold . These are historical commercial-trucking findings, not a current estimate for Matteson box truck operators. Source: FMCSA detention research For your business, the important questions are practical: What appointment time have you agreed to? When does billable detention begin under the agreement? What arrival and departure evidence is required? Who authorizes additional charges? What happens if the delay prevents your next pickup? Record detention requested, approved, and paid separately. An additional charge on an invoice is not collected income. 05 / Owner guide How much should you budget for box truck insurance? Use a quote based on your operation rather than another operator’s premium. Progressive identifies truck size, cargo, driving records, operating distance and location, coverage limits, and deductibles as factors affecting box truck insurance costs. Its guidance does not establish one price that applies to every box truck business. Source: Progressive Commercial Prepare these details before discussing coverage: The truck’s VIN, value, ownership, and financing information. Drivers and their driving histories. What you transport and the value of the goods. Typical routes, operating radius, and garaging location. Customer contracts and requested insurance limits. Your existing policy and renewal documents, if applicable. Compare more than the monthly payment. Review total premium, payment terms, limits, deductibles, exclusions, and whether the proposed coverage matches the work. Motive helps trucking businesses review vehicles, drivers, cargo, operating radius, contracts, and budget when considering coverage options. Explore Motive truck insurance 06 / Owner guide The Box Truck Week-in-Review Worksheet Review receipts, mileage, invoices, and collected payments together at the end of each week. Print / save worksheet as PDF Week of: __________________ Truck: __________________ Before expanding—or deciding the business can replace your job—close each week with a consistent record. Record What to enter Revenue billed Completed work invoiced during the week Cash collected Payments actually received, including earlier invoices Loaded miles Miles driven while carrying paying freight Empty miles Pickup travel, repositioning, and empty returns Fuel expense Actual fuel purchases Other trip expenses Tolls, parking, and job-specific charges Recurring cost allocation A consistent weekly share of recurring business costs Maintenance and reserves Actual repairs and separately identified reserve contributions Owner hours Driving, loading, dispatching, paperwork, and collections Calculate: Gross revenue per total mile = revenue billed ÷ total miles Deadhead percentage = empty miles ÷ total miles × 100 Operating cash movement = cash collected − cash paid out These figures answer different questions. Revenue per mile measures the work. Cash movement shows what happened to the bank balance. Neither, by itself, proves the business earned enough to pay the owner. 07 / Owner guide Is a box truck business profitable? It can be, but profitability depends on the relationship between collected revenue, operating expenses, truck ownership costs, and the work required to earn that revenue. Before leaving employment, compare the business with your current situation: What compensation would be available for your work? How many total hours would you spend earning it? What benefits would you need to replace? Could the business meet its obligations during repairs or slow collections? Would money remain for maintenance and eventual truck replacement? The goal is to build a business that can pay you consistently while remaining able to operate. 08 / Owner guide Frequently asked questions Should I calculate rates using loaded miles or total miles? Use total miles to evaluate the complete movement. Loaded-mile pricing can be useful for comparing offers, but it does not capture unpaid travel. Is money left after fuel my profit? No. Fuel is only one expense. Account for the remaining operating costs, recurring obligations, and the cost of your own work. Can another operator’s insurance payment tell me what mine will cost? It can provide context, but it cannot replace a quote. Differences in vehicles, drivers, cargo, routes, limits, and deductibles can affect pricing. What records should I keep from my first week? Keep load agreements, delivery records, invoices, payment records, mileage logs, fuel receipts, other expense receipts, and loading-delay documentation. 09 / Owner guide Review your coverage before committing to the work Bring Motive the details of the operation you plan to run: your truck, drivers, freight, routes, and customer requirements. pages.mainText: Car Hauling Insurance A guide to auto transport insurance questions, from truck and trailer protection to customer vehicle values and pickup-to-delivery responsibilities. Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance When you haul a vehicle, you are responsible for more than your truck and trailer. You are also responsible for somebody else's automobile. One load may represent tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in customer property. This guide explains the differences between commercial auto, cargo, equipment, and business liability considerations for vehicle transport operations. What is car hauling insurance? Car hauling insurance is commercial insurance structured around businesses transporting automobiles and other vehicles. Operations may include: Single-car hauling Multi-car hauling Auto transport Dealer vehicle transport Auction transport Vehicle relocation Enclosed vehicle transport Open vehicle transport Classic car transport Luxury vehicle transport Fleet vehicle relocation Interstate auto transport Each operation should be evaluated based on what is being transported and how. Commercial auto liability The power unit is still a commercial vehicle. Commercial auto liability can help address covered bodily injury and property damage resulting from the operation of insured commercial vehicles. The truck, trailer, driver, routes and operating radius should all be represented accurately. Motor truck cargo for vehicle transporters Cargo coverage is a major consideration for car haulers because the cargo is the customer's vehicle. The value of a load can increase quickly. Consider a trailer carrying: Several late-model vehicles Luxury vehicles Classic automobiles Dealer inventory Specialty vehicles A cargo limit that appears adequate for one type of load may be insufficient for another. Car haulers should evaluate: Maximum number of vehicles per load Average vehicle value Maximum vehicle value Maximum total load value Open versus enclosed transport Loading procedures Securement Storage Routes Deductibles Cargo exclusions The cargo limit should reflect real operations—not an arbitrary number chosen only to satisfy a certificate requirement. Physical damage for the truck and trailer Cargo coverage protects a different interest than physical damage coverage. Physical damage can help protect insured trucks and trailers against covered collision and comprehensive losses. A complete review should consider the value of: Power unit Trailer Specialized equipment Aftermarket additions Loading and unloading exposure Car hauling risk does not begin once the truck reaches highway speed. Damage can happen while a vehicle is: Driven onto the trailer Positioned Secured Moved between decks Unloaded Transferred Stored temporarily Loading procedures, driver experience and equipment condition all matter. Open vs. enclosed car hauling Open car carriers and enclosed transporters can have different exposures. Enclosed transport is often used for: Luxury automobiles Classic vehicles Exotic vehicles Collector cars Specialty vehicles Higher individual vehicle values should be discussed with the insurer. Do not assume a standard cargo limit automatically matches a high-value auto transport operation. Dealer and auction vehicle transport Car haulers may move vehicles for: Auto dealerships Dealer groups Auto auctions Fleet operators Rental companies Manufacturers Private customers Commercial contracts may establish their own insurance requirements. Compare requested limits and certificates with the actual loads, contracts, and policy wording. General liability Some vehicle transport businesses also have premises, loading areas or other operations outside normal highway transportation. General liability may help address certain covered third-party business claims not arising from auto liability. Workers' compensation Drivers and employees may be injured while loading, securing, inspecting or transporting vehicles. Workers' compensation should be considered based on staffing and applicable state requirements. Umbrella or excess liability Larger auto transport operations and certain contracts may require higher liability limits. Umbrella or excess liability may be appropriate depending on the underlying coverage and business requirements. Documents for a car hauling insurance review Organize the following information before comparing coverage: Number of trucks Number of trailers Truck values Trailer values Driver information USDOT information when applicable Operating radius States of operation Types of vehicles transported Maximum vehicle value Maximum load value Average number of vehicles per load Open or enclosed transport Customers and contracts Annual mileage Loss history Current insurance Requested cargo limit Renewal date What affects car hauling insurance cost? Insurance carriers may consider: Equipment Drivers Operating history Radius Claims Cargo values Vehicle types transported Trailer configuration Number of vehicles hauled Contracts Annual mileage Coverage limits Deductibles Starting a car hauling business? Do not build the business first and ask about insurance at the last minute. Before accepting your first transport job, understand: What truck you will operate What trailer you will use What vehicles you will transport Where you will operate How much cargo value you may carry What contracts require Which filings or authority may apply to your operation What information insurers will request Insurance is part of the operating model. Resolve the insurance questions alongside equipment, operating authority, and contract planning before accepting a transport assignment. From one trailer to a car-hauling fleet Growth creates new complexity. Additional trucks mean additional drivers. Additional trailers mean additional values. Larger contracts can increase cargo concentration. Longer routes increase mileage. Higher-end clients can increase vehicle values. A growing car hauling business should review insurance as those variables change. Protect the equipment and the vehicles you are paid to move The truck matters. The trailer matters. The driver matters. The customer's vehicle matters. Car hauling insurance should account for all four. Compare coverage against the actual equipment, routes, vehicle values, and responsibilities in the operation. Coverage comparison Separate the equipment from the customer vehicles Situation Review area Question to ask Power unit in a road accident Commercial auto liability Which insured vehicles and transportation activities are described? Damage to your truck or trailer Physical damage How are equipment values, deductibles, and modifications addressed? Damage to customer vehicles Motor truck cargo or applicable transit coverage What property, activities, limits, exclusions, and valuation wording apply? Loading, unloading, or a transfer The applicable policy wording When does coverage attach and end, and which handling activities are included? A dealer or auction agreement Contract and insurance documentation Do requested limits and obligations match the loads and policy terms? A practical example Example: calculate the total value on one load For illustration, six customer vehicles valued at $40,000 each create $240,000 in combined vehicle value. That arithmetic is a starting point for a cargo-limit discussion, not a recommended limit or a promise of payment. Check any per-vehicle restrictions, valuation terms, deductibles, exclusions, and maximum exposure on other loads. A load with fewer luxury vehicles can be worth more than a full load of lower-value vehicles. Common mistakes to avoid Confusing a filing requirement with cargo protection Regulatory filings and protection for customer vehicles answer different questions. Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance Non-emergency medical transportation businesses do more than move passengers from one address to another. Your drivers may transport seniors, Medicaid members, passengers using wheelchairs, people traveling to dialysis or therapy appointments, and individuals who need additional assistance entering or exiting a vehicle. That creates a different risk profile than an ordinary commercial vehicle. This guide explains the coverage categories, operational details, and contract questions that belong in an NEMT insurance review. Commercial auto. Passenger exposure. Wheelchair transportation. Drivers. Contracts. Business liability. One insurance conversation. What is NEMT insurance? NEMT insurance is commercial insurance structured around businesses providing non-emergency medical transportation. It may apply to operations such as: Non-emergency medical transportation Wheelchair transportation Ambulette services Senior transportation Medicaid transportation Dialysis transportation Medical appointment transportation Mobility-assisted transportation Private-pay medical transportation The appropriate insurance program depends on the vehicles you use, who you transport, where you operate, how drivers are hired, whether passengers require assistance, and the contracts your company accepts. That is why an NEMT operation should not be treated like a generic commercial auto account. What insurance does an NEMT business need? Commercial Auto Liability Commercial auto liability is a core component of most NEMT insurance programs. It can help address covered bodily injury or property damage claims resulting from the operation of insured vehicles. The vehicles, passenger capacity, operating radius, driver history and use of each vehicle can all affect the insurance review. Physical Damage Your vehicles are essential business assets. Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles against covered collision and comprehensive losses such as theft, vandalism, fire, weather damage and other covered events. Passenger Exposure NEMT businesses carry people. That distinction matters. Passengers may have mobility limitations, use wheelchairs or other equipment, or require assistance entering and exiting a vehicle. An insurance review should account for the passenger exposure created by the services the business actually provides. General Liability Not every business claim begins with a vehicle accident. General liability can help address certain covered third-party bodily injury or property damage claims arising from business operations outside the normal commercial auto exposure. Workers' Compensation Drivers and transportation staff can face workplace injuries while assisting passengers, operating accessibility equipment, entering facilities, loading mobility devices or performing other duties. Workers' compensation should be reviewed based on the company's employees, state requirements and operational structure. Umbrella or Excess Liability Some NEMT operations, contracts or larger fleets may need liability limits beyond the underlying policies. Umbrella or excess liability may provide additional protection above certain eligible underlying liability policies. Wheelchair transportation changes the risk A wheelchair-accessible transportation company is not simply operating a van with more equipment. The operation may involve: Wheelchair ramps Hydraulic lifts Securement systems Passenger restraints Mobility devices Driver assistance Loading and unloading passengers Specialized vehicle modifications The condition and use of this equipment can become part of the overall risk. Map the entire passenger journey, from approaching the vehicle to arriving at the destination. Identify who assists the passenger, which equipment is used, and where responsibility changes hands. Medicaid and contract transportation Some NEMT providers perform trips through Medicaid transportation programs, transportation brokers, healthcare networks, facilities or other contractual arrangements. Those contracts can establish insurance requirements that go beyond simply having a commercial auto policy. Your operation may need to provide certificates of insurance or demonstrate particular liability limits before a contract can be activated or renewed. Requirements can vary by state, program, broker and contract. Compare each written insurance requirement with the declarations, coverage forms, and endorsements in the actual policy. A certificate alone does not resolve every coverage question. What affects the cost of NEMT insurance? NEMT insurance pricing is not determined by one factor. Insurers may consider: Number of vehicles Vehicle type Passenger capacity Vehicle age and value Wheelchair accessibility Operating radius States of operation Number of drivers Driver experience Motor vehicle records Loss history Annual mileage Type of passengers transported Contracts Hours of operation Business experience Coverage limits The goal should not be to find an insurance policy based on one generic price. The goal is to build an NEMT insurance program that reflects the operation being insured. Starting an NEMT business? Insurance should be part of the business planning process. Before accepting transportation contracts, understand what your vehicles will be used for and what coverage those contracts may require. Questions to document before reviewing coverage: What type of passengers will you transport? Will you provide wheelchair transportation? How many vehicles will you operate? What vehicles are you purchasing? How many passengers can each vehicle carry? Will transportation be private-pay, Medicaid, facility-based or contract work? How far will your vehicles travel? Will you cross state lines? Who will drive? Do your drivers assist passengers? Do you currently have contracts requiring specific insurance limits? Those answers help move the conversation from “I need commercial auto insurance” to a real NEMT insurance review. Growing NEMT fleets A transportation company with one vehicle has a different insurance challenge from a company operating fifteen. Growth can add: More vehicles More drivers More passengers More facilities More contracts Higher mileage Additional certificates More claims exposure Additional management responsibilities Insurance should be reviewed as the operation changes. Compare the current operation with the description used when the policies were issued. A new service area, additional passenger assistance, or a larger fleet can change the questions that need to be reviewed. Key takeaways for NEMT operators Your passengers depend on your business to get them where they need to go. Your business depends on the vehicles and people that make those trips possible. A useful review connects the coverage documents to the entire transportation operation. Vehicles. Passengers. Drivers. Contracts. Business risk. Damage to your own van Physical damage How are vehicle value, deductible, and accessibility modifications addressed? Passenger assistance Service responsibilities and coverage wording How are boarding, unloading, wheelchair securement, and assistance away from the van treated? Employee injury Workers’ compensation Are the duties of drivers and passenger-assistance staff accurately described? A new facility contract Policy limits and endorsements Do the written requirements match the coverage actually issued? A practical example Example: a wheelchair-accessible van joins the fleet An operator adds an accessible van to a fleet previously used for ambulatory passengers. Listing the vehicle is only one step. Record the lift or ramp, securement equipment, passenger assistance tasks, seating configuration, and any new facility agreement. Ask how each change is reflected in the policy. This example illustrates a review process; it does not establish whether a particular loss would be covered. Common mistakes to avoid Confusing the passenger benefit with business insurance Medicaid transportation eligibility and an operator’s commercial insurance are different topics. A covered patient trip does not establish that the operator’s business policy addresses every service it performs. Reviewing only the time spent driving Boarding, transferring assistance, securing equipment, and leaving the vehicle can introduce questions that are missed when the review starts and ends with a vehicle list. Treating a certificate as the whole policy A certificate summarizes selected information. Review the applicable forms and endorsements when a contract calls for a particular protection. Wheelchair transportation introduces additional operational considerations including mobility equipment, vehicle modifications, passenger assistance, lifts, ramps and securement systems. These details should be discussed when reviewing coverage. Does Medicaid require NEMT insurance? Medicaid transportation programs and transportation brokers can establish provider and insurance requirements. Requirements vary by state, program and contract, so operators should review the specific requirements that apply to their business. What should a new NEMT business review before its first trip? Document the planned vehicles, passenger capacity, accessibility equipment, driver responsibilities, routes, and contracts. Freight Broker Financial Responsibility Bonds and trusts A BMC-84 surety bond provides financial security for payments owed to shippers or motor carriers when a broker fails to meet its covered transportation obligations. The provider files the appropriate bond or trust form with FMCSA. The role of trust in transportation compliance Compare the funding obligations as well as the fees. A BMC-85 commits qualifying assets to the trust, which can affect the funds available to run the business. With a BMC-84, an approved applicant generally pays a premium rather than depositing the full bond amount. Underwriting may also require collateral. Review indemnity and reimbursement terms: paying a premium does not eliminate the broker's obligations for covered claims. BMC-85 assets are limited to cash, irrevocable letters of credit from federally insured depository institutions, and U.S. Treasury bonds, and must be convertible to cash within seven calendar days. Loan and finance companies are no longer eligible BMC-85 trustees. The rules also address provider reporting, financial failure and suspension when available security falls below $75,000. Respond promptly to any FMCSA notice and follow the current regulatory procedures. These changes did not replace the $75,000 security requirement. The whole operation Towing Creates More Than One Insurance Risk A towing company does more than operate a commercial truck. Your business may pick up disabled vehicles, transport customer vehicles, perform roadside assistance, recover damaged vehicles, store vehicles, work with motor clubs, or participate in police and municipal towing programs. You may hear the terms car hauling , vehicle transport, and towing used to describe similar types of work. Most customers simply call it towing. In the insurance industry, car hauling or vehicle transportation may also be used when describing businesses that move customer vehicles. Commercial Auto Liability Commercial auto liability can address covered bodily injury or property damage claims arising from operation of insured commercial vehicles. Physical Damage Physical damage can help protect an insured tow truck, rollback, or wrecker against covered collision and comprehensive losses, subject to policy terms and deductibles. On-Hook Coverage On-hook coverage is designed to address covered damage to a customer's vehicle while it is being towed or transported by the towing operation. Garagekeepers Coverage Garagekeepers coverage addresses customer vehicles being stored or kept in the towing company's care at its location, subject to policy terms. General Liability General liability can address certain covered third-party bodily injury or property damage exposures arising from business activities outside normal vehicle operation.
